expectations.text: No U/D cycle is kept, or every kept cycle documents attempted flips of each link with expert-confirmed rejection reasons
expectations.evidence: Validator v3 shows that 2 direct cycles ('RULE ud-cycle: Billing -> Complaints -> Billing', 'RULE ud-cycle: Billing -> Scheduling -> Billing') and 4 indirect ones were kept. The report's 'Breaking cycles' table lists flips with answer references (R6-3, R7-2, R7-3, R6-4, R6-2, R7-4), so the documentation exists. The rejections are not expert-confirmed rejections of the flips, though. (1) The links that create both direct cycles rest on improvised answers that are not in the fact sheet: R3-1 'A student with an "unpaid" lesson can't book again [improvised]' and R6-4 'Complaints needs ... what was charged from Billing [improvised]'. (2) The concrete alternatives were never put to the expert, for example a Billing-side refund cap so Complaints needs no ChargeDetails (the baseline run got the expert to accept exactly that), or a Scheduling-owned booking-block input. (3) The rating-in-request flip was not asked neutrally, unlike the held-count flip in R7-1. (4) The combination cycles are dismissed with 'as above'. On a literal reading this is close to a pass; on substance, against a rule that a two-way U/D is a design error, it is not.

notes: CYCLES. The kept direct cycles are weakly justified under the trainer's rules (U/D both ways between two contexts = design error). (a) Billing<->Complaints: RefundDecisions is a command 'refund lesson L, amount A' that Billing executes, and ChargeDetails is a read of Billing's data. Both are naturally Billing-upstream: Billing offers an OHS/PL 'refund' API plus charge lookup, and Complaints is downstream with an ACL. Sending a command to an upstream's API does not make the sender upstream. The run rejected this with R7-3 ('doesn't fill in anyone else's form'), which is the expert's choice in a binary 'whose terms' question about a two-field message, not a structural fact. The baseline also showed that ChargeDetails can simply be dropped: the complaint carries the lesson ref and Billing caps the refund at the charged amount, which the expert accepted. So this cycle should have been broken. (b) Billing<->Scheduling: LessonOutcomes (Scheduling upstream) is solid in the fact sheet ('Billing needs ... the lesson facts'). The back link StudentPaymentStanding comes from an improvised fact. Better options: treat 'Lesson Unpaid/Paid' as event notification into a Scheduling-owned language, where Scheduling publishes a 'StudentBookingBlock' input/OHS that Billing feeds (Billing downstream, keeping 'booking keeps its own note'); or, if the teams really co-evolve both directions, model it honestly as a Partnership (internal teams; the trainer's rules don't forbid it) instead of two opposing C/S arrows. A merge is wrong (different teams, rules and clocks). (c) The indirect cycles (Pricing->Scheduling->Reviews->Pricing; Complaints->T&S->Scheduling->Complaints) are mostly benign. Each arrow is a narrow, different language, and the chains are event flows, so keeping them with documented reasons is acceptable. SKILL GUIDANCE: The skill should treat a DIRECT two-way U/D as a hard error that can't be kept. It must be resolved by (1) re-reading one side as a command to, or query of, the other's API (direction follows whose model is the contract, not message direction); (2) moving a responsibility or dropping a dependency (could the data travel in the message, or could the upstream enforce the cap?); (3) declaring Partnership; (4) a merge as the last resort. INDIRECT cycles should be a review warning: check each arrow is a model dependency rather than plain event flow, and keep them with a documented reason. The skill should also forbid justifying a kept cycle by an [improvised] answer, or by the expert's pick in a binary 'whose terms' question, and require the alternative flip itself to be put to the expert. The map critics accepted the cycles ('cycles accepted'); the critic prompt should challenge every direct cycle. EVAL CRITIQUE: assertion 8 can be satisfied by paperwork; split it into 'no direct U/D cycle kept' (strict) and 'indirect cycles documented'. Assertion 2 passes even though Billing no longer depends on Pricing directly; consider whether that is intended. Not covered: whether kept dependencies rest on [improvised] facts. Cost: 262k tokens and 1154 s versus the baseline's 77k tokens and 242 s, for 9 expert rounds. Mechanical grading: 9/10, with the failure on the direct ud-cycle. Canvases, the report and C/S+ACL defaults are clearly better than the baseline.
